transcript:
Meeting header: 
- Date/Time: 2027-05-04 16:00 PT
- Duration: ~68 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Nora Patel (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (CTO, Architecta.io), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra), Leah Morales (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Redwood ran an Optimize console walkthrough focused on batching and KV prefetch recommendations for Architecta's conversational assistant workload. Discussed tradeoffs between aggressive prefix prefetch, session caching, and batching window sizes. Reviewed cost model scenarios and identified two likely pilots: hosted with dedicated burst + prefix prefetch, or private VPC with quantized model and session cache. Action items and next steps agreed.

Topics covered:
- Baseline metrics and SLOs (latency p50/p95, throughput)
- Prefix/KV prefetch patterns and cache TTLs
- Batching window, concurrency, and token economy tradeoffs
- Model variants (quantized vs FP16) and fallback routing
- Sandbox sim and cost spreadsheet walkthrough

Key links mentioned:
- Deck: https://redwood.local/decks/optimize-prefetch-arch-2027 (note: link shorthand)
- Cost spreadsheet: https://redwood.local/spreadsheets/arch-cost-model-2027
- Sandbox: https://sandbox.redwood-demo/architecta/

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, we've got Diego and Nora from the SE team, welcome Architecta folks.
[00:12] Oliver Grant: Hey thanks, excited to see how we can get our token costs down, and also keep latency under, you know, 150 ms p95 if possible.
[00:24] Diego Ramos: Great, yeah we'll try to hit both, today is an Optimize console walkthrough, so we'll show the prefetched KV and batching knobs, do a couple of sims, and then hand off the cost model.
[00:36] Priya Nair: Quick context - our assistant is multi-turn, average prompt + history is ~320 tokens, but about 30% of sessions are long, like 1.5k tokens. Peak concurrency is about 900 sessions, average 420.
[00:53] Nora Patel: Got it, the long tail shapes the caching strategy; we often recommend prefix caching for the stable system prompts and early-turn content.
[01:06] Samir Patel: We run everything in a VPC, we have strict KMS keys, SOC2 in progress, and we can't forward raw customer data outside their region. 
[01:18] Maya Chen: Thanks Samir, we'll call out VPC/private implications. Quick show of the console - jumping into the Optimize tab, here's the batching slider, KV prefetch policy, and the cost sim area.
[01:36] Diego Ramos: First demo scenario: conservative prefetch — only prefetch when session re-use probability > 0.6 and TTL 30 minutes, batching target 16 tokens window. This reduces waste on rare sessions.
[01:50] Oliver Grant: When you say prefetch, is that the same as the prefix cache you mentioned on the docs? Sometimes I see "prefix cash" or "KV cash" in our notes, haha.
[02:01] Maya Chen: Yeah small transcription issue in docs occasionally - it's KV cache / prefix cache. In practice we precompute KV states for the top-N session prefixes.
[02:12] Priya Nair: Do you have heuristics for deciding top-N? We have some prefixes that vary by user name or product id so not sure how to generalize.
[02:23] Diego Ramos: We usually filter on normalized prefixes - strip session ids, mask PII, then rank by frequency. For Architecta you'd pick top 500-2k depending on memory budget.
[02:36] [02:36] (crosstalk)
[02:47] Nora Patel: Important to consider KV memory vs throughput, too much prefetch can inflate memory footprint and reduce batch coalescing.
[02:58] Samir Patel: What's the typical memory per prefix entry? ballpark numbers help.
[03:08] Diego Ramos: On our runtime with quantized models, a prefix KV entry is ~1.2MB for 8-bit KV, ~3MB for FP16. That's rough, depends on sequence length and key/value sizes.
[03:26] Priya Nair: So if we did 2k prefixes that's ~2.4GB which is ok for our dedicated pool. But what's the savings in token cost?
[03:38] Diego Ramos: In the cost sim we ran earlier, with 2k high-frequency prefixes you can save up to 18-25% of per-token compute cost in the steady state because you avoid recomputing the first 50-200 tokens each session.
[03:53] Oliver Grant: And latencies? Prefetch adds memory read but should reduce overall generation time for later tokens, correct?
[04:03] Diego Ramos: Exactly. You'll see p50 drop for mid-turn responses; p95 depends on batching and KV hit rate. If you prefetch aggressively and have high hit rate, p95 improves.
[04:18] Maya Chen: Now switching to a more aggressive scenario - prefetch everything for known system prompts, TTL 4 hours, batch target 48, allow small extra latency for initial token to batch.
[04:33] Leah Morales: For product, what I care about is tail latency and cost predictability. If we increase batch target to 48 will that spike p95 under load?
[04:44] Diego Ramos: There's a tradeoff: larger batch targets increase throughput efficiency and reduce unit cost, but when traffic is bursty it can add queueing latency. We recommend dynamic batching: set an upper batch size but enable concurrency SLOs so critical routes bypass batching.
[05:02] Priya Nair: Can we route urgent user actions to a low-latency path and less-critical assistants to the batched path?
[05:09] Nora Patel: Yes, routing policies in the console let you create route tags (e.g., interactive vs background) and apply different batching/prefetch configs per route.
[05:20] Oliver Grant: How do we simulate our mixed workload?
[05:23] Diego Ramos: Use the sandbox sim link I shared, upload your 7-day traffic and the console will run a sim across different configs and produce cost/latency curves. We'll provision a sandbox with your traffic after you share the histograms.
[05:39] Maya Chen: Let's walk through the cost spreadsheet quick - baseline hosted FP16, no prefetch, batching 12 -> that's our baseline row. Then we have scenario A: moderate prefetch + batch 24; scenario B: heavy prefetch + batch 48 with dedicated capacity.
[05:55] Priya Nair: The spreadsheet assumptions - what's the tokenization model used? Are you assuming 1 token = 4 characters?
[06:03] Diego Ramos: The sheet uses model-specific tokenization approximations, but for a quick baseline we used ~3.4 chars/token. We'll parameterize that when you upload your prompts; that can change cost by ~6-8%.
[06:17] [06:17] (brief pause)
[06:28] Samir Patel: Our security checklist — KMS, SAML SSO, audit logs retention, and data residency. How does prefetch affect PII handling?
[06:40] Maya Chen: Good question. Prefetch must be done on normalized prefixes with PII masked. We also support customer-managed keys for private deployments; prefetch artifacts can be stored encrypted at rest with your KMS.
[06:54] Oliver Grant: You mentioned private deployment earlier — if we go private in our region, do we lose any Optimize console features?
[07:02] Nora Patel: Private has the same control plane features; some advanced sandboxing for shared telemetry is limited, but most of the Optimize engine runs locally and the console can point at the private control plane.
[07:15] Leah Morales: In terms of rollout, how would a canary look? We want to try prefetch on 10% of traffic first.
[07:23] Diego Ramos: Canary policy is configurable: you can do route-based rollouts, percentage, and A/B buckets. For prefetch we often recommend starting with 5-10% of sessions that match high-frequency prefixes, validate latency and correctness, then expand.
[07:40] Priya Nair: How do we validate correctness? We care about hallucinations after prefetching — could state in the KV introduce stale context?
[07:50] Diego Ramos: Prefetch keys are built from sanitized, canonicalized prefixes. We keep versioning and TTLs; if you detect hallucination patterns linked to stale prefix, you can adjust TTL or add a freshness check that falls back to on-the-fly generation. We also surface diffs in the Console evals tab.
[08:07] Oliver Grant: Any caveats with quantized models? We currently plan to use an 8-bit quantized variant.
[08:14] Diego Ramos: Quantization is great for cost, but KV representation differs vs FP16 slightly. You might see micro-diffs in probabilities but usually no user-visible regressions. We recommend running the quality evals in the console to compare outputs across model variants.
[08:29] Maya Chen: Ok let's run the cost sim live — pulling up the sandbox sim, loading your traffic profile (we used a synthetic example here), baseline shows $X per million tokens at batch 12. Switching to scenario A with 2k prefix prefetch and batch 24 shows ~15% savings; scenario B with heavy prefetch + batch 48 shows ~28% savings but requires dedicated nodes and ~3GB extra KV memory per node.
[08:58] Leah Morales: Those numbers look good. For procurement we'll need a clear decision path: pilot -> enterprise contract?
[09:07] Maya Chen: Typical flow: pilot (4-6 weeks) on dedicated burst or private depending on controls, then enterprise commit if savings meet threshold. We'll provide a pilot plan and pricing options.
[09:18] [09:18] (unrelated background noise)
[09:26] Priya Nair: Quick question on metrics - do you measure cache hit rate and cost-per-request per route?
[09:33] Nora Patel: Yes, Console telemetry shows per-route hit rate, average latency, tokens saved, and cost delta. We can create a dashboard and share read-only links.
[09:45] Samir Patel: For the pilot, what infra changes are needed? VPC peering and some IAM roles?
[09:51] Diego Ramos: VPC peering and KMS access for private deployments; for Hosted Dedicated we'll need IP allowlist and optional VPC peering for egress. We'll send a deployment checklist.
[10:03] Oliver Grant: Are there any competitors that do this same mix of prefetch and batching out of the box?
[10:09] Maya Chen: Some vendors offer batching but not prefix-aware prefetching with integrated cost sims; others do prefetch as a custom layer. We mentioned OpenAI and Cohere earlier but they don't ship the same runtime + console experience across hosted and private.
[10:24] Priya Nair: Curious about fallback policies — if prefetch fails or capacity spikes, do you automatically route to smaller model/FP16?
[10:33] Diego Ramos: Yes, we support automatic fallback policies by cost or latency thresholds. You can set priority: primary model, fallback quantized variant, then micro model or a cached sentence fallback.
[10:45] Leah Morales: That helps with reliability. Any final risk items?
[10:49] Nora Patel: Watch out for overprefetching and lock-in to particular prefixes; keep an ops playbook for pruning low-value prefixes. Also monitor for drift in prefix frequency.
[11:01] Maya Chen: OK let's recap next steps — Maya will send the cost spreadsheet and pilot pricing, Diego will spin up the sandbox and run a throughput sim targeting 2k RPS, Priya will share histograms and prompts, Samir will confirm KMS/VPC constraints, and we'll schedule the latency deep-dive.
[11:18] Oliver Grant: Great, thanks everyone. Appreciate the concrete numbers.
[11:22] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and attach the sheets and checklist.
[11:28] (meeting ends)

End of transcript.
